doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Accompanying singers and Tony Bennett
summary: Comping for vocalists means listening and playing counterpoint; Tony Bennett offered him Ralph Sharon's job and later asked for lessons.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: This is great. A little while ago you used the word “comping.” I wanted to ask you about comping behind Joe Williams and Nancy Wilson and Jimmy Witherspoon. How does a piano player learn to be an accompanist that vocalists want to work with?

Well without getting real technical, the main way would be listen. Listening. And you have to have your voice leading together so that you’re playing contrapuntally. So the basis of simple counterpoint is when the main theme is moving, you’re standing still. When that stops then you move. And so I would listen to something the vocalist did and then play in between the phrases, and then we’d lock up together. And so the singers all like to work with me. Nancy, she told somebody in Florida, “Mike Longo really knows how to play for a singer” or something like that. And I stopped doing that. When I first left Dizzy I wanted to do my own thing. Tony Bennett wanted me to replace Ralph — what was the guy?

Yeah. And I didn’t take the gig because I wanted to do my own thing man. I told him I would fill in for him until he could get somebody. But then Tony called me when John Bunch died. At the funeral. He called me the next day, he said, “Man I want to study piano with you, because I always wanted to play like you were doing.” And so he was supposed to call me back on Monday and I never heard from him again. But the main thing is you have to listen and move when they’re moving — when they’re moving you’re playing slower notes and when they’re playing slower notes you’re playing faster notes.

Do you like to see a lead sheet — maybe you’re obviously way beyond this. But when I play behind a singer I kind of like to know what note they’re going to be singing — at least a lead sheet of how the song normally goes.

Well sure. Well you look at a lead sheet as information. And so yeah. Look man, Aaron Copland said, “The art of classical music is the art of melody.” So melody is number one. And so if the singer is singing the melody you don’t want to be playing something that’s going to clash with that. And so if you’re playing contrapuntally you’re playing something that complements. And so there was a lady — I’m not going to mention her name. I played this gig with her, man. And she’s playing these tunes and she had no double bars or anything, just changes running. It’s like reading something with no punctuation in it. And it sounded terrible. And then I looked at the real music and I said, “Oh you should have put a double bar here man, ‘cause I didn’t know that this was a new section.” And no melody, just the changes.

And so instead of playing the song you end up playing F7, B flat 7, you’re not really playing the music, you’re playing the changes. And so we have to be involved with — there are five elements to music. Melody, harmony, rhythm, counterpoint, and form. And so you have to have yourself trained to deal with all five of those things. And if the singer is the melody then you’re doing the counterpoint, the rhythm — and so rhythm is primary. In our music rhythm and melody almost mean the same thing. Dizzy used to use the term the “melodization of rhythm.”
So it’s simple. [scats] Right? So you have to listen man.
